overview.why: Anything you do twice by hand should be a script. Bash is the glue of DevOps: deploy scripts, backups, health checks and CI steps are all shell scripts. A script that fails silently is worse than no script, so this unit teaches the habits (strict mode, traps, argument checking) that make scripts safe to run on real servers.
prerequisites: Linux basics: files, permissions, pipes and cron.
outcomes: Start every script with `set -euo pipefail` and explain what each flag protects you from
Clean up temporary files and lock files even when a script crashes, using `trap`
Accept options like `-e production -v` with `getopts` and print a helpful usage message
Write a disk and log monitoring script that alerts when a limit is crossed
Quote variables correctly so a space in a filename does not break your script
overview.placementTip: A very common take-home task is "write a script that checks disk usage and warns above 80%". Be ready to write it from memory, with error handling.

sections.title: Defensive Bash Scripting (set -euo pipefail)

content.value: By default, Bash continues running a script even if a command fails! Imagine a backup script: `cd /backup_dir` fails (directory missing), and the next line is `rm -rf *`. Standard Bash will run `rm -rf *` inside your home directory and delete everything! Scared?
To prevent disaster, every professional production Bash script MUST start with the **Unofficial Bash Strict Mode**: `set -euo pipefail`.

content.title: Strict Mode Explanation
content.value:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

# -e : Exit immediately if ANY command returns a non-zero exit code
# -u : Exit immediately if an UNSET variable is referenced
# -o pipefail : If any command in a pipeline fails (e.g. cat bad | grep foo), fail the WHOLE pipeline
Interview favorite: 'What does set -euo pipefail do?' Explain each letter (-e, -u, -o pipefail). Mentioning this in any Linux/DevOps interview proves you have real-world production experience!

keyPoints: `set -e` stops at the first failing command; `-u` treats an unset variable as an error; `-o pipefail` fails a pipe if any part fails.
Check inputs first and fail early with a clear message and a non-zero exit code.

quiz.question: What happens when 'set -e' is enabled in a Bash script?
options: The script exits immediately if any command returns a non-zero (failure) exit code
The script runs in the background
quiz.explanation: 'set -e' tells Bash to immediately abort script execution if any single command fails. This prevents cascading errors and accidental file deletion.

sections.title: Error Trapping & Cleanup Hooks

content.value: When a script crashes or exits, it might leave temporary files or lock files behind. The `trap` command registers a cleanup function that automatically executes whenever the script exits, dies, or receives a signal.

content.title: Bash Trap Cleanup Lifecycle
content.value:
graph TD
    START["🚀 Script Begins"] --> TEMP["Create /tmp/lock.pid"]
    TEMP --> REG["trap cleanup EXIT INT TERM"]
    REG --> EXEC["Perform operations..."]
    EXEC -->|Script Exits or Crashes| TRAP["🧹 Trap Triggers: cleanup()"]
    TRAP --> RM["Delete /tmp/lock.pid"]
    RM --> FINISH["🏁 Clean Shutdown"]
    style TRAP fill:#1a2332,stroke:#00d4ff,color:#e2e8f0
    style RM fill:#1a2332,stroke:#10b981,color:#e2e8f0

content.title: Complete Robust Script Template
content.value:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

# Create temporary file
TEMP_FILE=$(mktemp /tmp/myapp.XXXXXX)

# Cleanup function
cleanup() {
  echo "Cleaning up temporary files..."
  rm -f "$TEMP_FILE"
}

# Register trap on EXIT, INT (Ctrl+C), TERM
trap cleanup EXIT INT TERM

echo "Processing data into $TEMP_FILE..."
# Do work here...

keyPoints: `trap 'cleanup' EXIT` runs your cleanup however the script ends.
Use `mktemp` for temporary files and remove them in the trap.
A lock file stops two copies of a job running at once; the trap removes it.

quiz.question: What is the primary use case of the 'trap' command in Bash?
options: To execute a cleanup function automatically when a script terminates or crashes
quiz.explanation: 'trap' registers handlers for signals (like EXIT, SIGINT, SIGTERM). It guarantees that temporary files, locks, or sockets are cleaned up regardless of how the script ends.

sections.title: Argument Parsing ($1, $@, getopts)

content.value: Production automation scripts accept command-line flags (e.g. `./deploy.sh -e production -v 1.2.0`). Bash provides built-in positional variables (`$1`, `$2`, `$@`) and the `getopts` built-in tool for robust argument handling.

content.title: getopts Argument Parsing Example

keyPoints: `$1`, `$2` are positional arguments, `$@` is all of them, `$#` is how many.
`getopts` handles flags such as `-e prod` the standard way.
Print usage and exit 1 when arguments are missing, so mistakes are obvious.

quiz.question: In Bash, what does '$@' represent?
options: The exit code of the last command
All positional command-line arguments passed to the script
The Process ID (PID) of the script
quiz.explanation: '$@' expands to a list of all positional parameters passed to the script, preserving individual quotes and spaces.

sections.title: Automated Disk & Log Monitoring Script

content.value: One of the most common real-world interview coding tasks is: 'Write a script that monitors disk space and sends an alert if usage exceeds 80%.' Here is the production-grade implementation.

content.title: Disk Space Monitor Script
content.value:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

THRESHOLD=80
EMAIL="ops-alerts@company.com"

df -H | grep -vE '^Filesystem|tmpfs|cdrom' | awk '{ print $5 " " $1 }' | while read -r output; do
  usep=$(echo "$output" | awk '{ print $1}' | cut -d'%' -f1)
  partition=$(echo "$output" | awk '{ print $2 }')
  
  if [ "$usep" -ge "$THRESHOLD" ]; then
    echo "[ALERT] Partition '$partition' is at $usep% usage on $(hostname) as of $(date)"
  fi
done

keyPoints: `df -h` and `awk` pull out the usage number; compare it with a threshold using `-gt`.
Send alerts (mail, webhook) and also write to a log so there is a record.
Run it from cron and test the failure path, not only the happy path.

quiz.question: How do you extract just the numeric percentage from '85%' in Bash?
quiz.explanation: 'cut -d"%" -f1' splits the text by the '%' delimiter and returns field 1 (the number 85).

cheatsheet.title: Bash scripting cheat sheet
rows: First line: which interpreter runs the script
Strict mode: stop on errors, unset variables and failed pipes
Use a default when the variable is empty
First argument / all arguments / how many / last exit code
Always clean up when the script ends
Capture normal output and errors together
